ABSTRACT: We present a quantum-classical hybrid algorithm for
calculating the ground state and its energy of the quantum many-
body Hamiltonian by proposing an adaptive construction of a
quantum state for the quantum-selected configuration interaction
(QSCI) method. QSCI allows us to select important electronic
configurations in the system to perform configuration interaction
(CI) calculation (subspace diagonalization of the Hamiltonian) by
sampling measurement for a proper input quantum state on a
quantum computer, but how we prepare a desirable input state
remains a challenge. We propose an adaptive construction of the
input state for QSCI in which we run QSCI repeatedly to grow the
input state iteratively. We numerically illustrate that our method, dubbed ADAPT-QSCI, can yield accurate ground-state energies for
small molecules, including a noisy situation for eight qubits where error rates of two-qubit gates and the measurement are both as
large as 1%. ADAPT-QSCI serves as a promising method to take advantage of current noisy quantum devices and pushes forward its
application to quantum chemistry.

          ML/MM Free Energy Calculations

João Morado,† Kirill Zinovjev,‡ Lester O. Hedges,¶ Daniel J. Cole,∗,§ and Julien

                                         Michel∗,†

                                         Abstract

       Hybrid ML/MM approaches that combine machine learning (ML) potentials with

    molecular mechanics (MM) potentials offer a promising balance between computational

    cost and accuracy. Most ML/MM simulations reported to date employ mechanical

    embedding schemes, and rely on Lennard-Jones and Coulomb potentials to model in-

    termolecular interactions between the ML and MM regions. A promising approach to

    improving ML/MM schemes is to use electrostatic embedding, where polarization ef-

    fects on the ML region by the MM region are explicitly incorporated. The electrostatic

    machine learning embedding (EMLE) method has been developed for this purpose.

    Here, we compute absolute hydration free energies for a set of small organic molecules

    to derive robust methodologies for training EMLE models using quantum mechani-

    cal data. We establish protocols for fine-tuning the static and induced components of

                                              1
       electrostatic interactions and evaluate the accuracy limits of fitting these components

      to first-principles calculations. We also introduce an empirical adjustment to enhance

      agreement with experimental results, strengthening the competitiveness of ML/MM

      simulations relative to state-of-the-art methods. Overall, our findings provide valu-

      able insights into the challenges and opportunities of electrostatic embedding ML/MM

      simulations, and offer strategies for achieving robust modeling of classes of drug-like

      molecules where the accuracy of conventional MM force fields fall short.



Introduction

Since the advent of machine learning potentials (MLPs), the field of molecular simulations
has undergone significant transformations. MLPs have the potential to match the accuracy
of quantum mechanical (QM) calculations while being orders of magnitude more computa-
tionally efficient. 1 Several transferable MLPs have been developed in recent years for organic
molecules, among which ANI-2x, 2 MACE-OFF, 3 AceFF, 4,5 and AIMNet 6,7 are some of the
most popular. To leverage the capabilities MLPs have to offer, methodologies are being
developed to integrate them into existing simulation software, 8–10 and entirely new tools are
being created. 11–13
   Because the computational cost of MLPs remains higher than that of molecular mechan-
ics (MM) force fields (FFs), there are not yet any long timescale validations of MLP protein
FFs. Therefore, recent advancements aimed at enabling and enhancing the performance
of hybrid machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) simulations are of particular
importance for biomolecular studies, where reliable and often long-timescale simulations
are essential. These developments in both methodology and digital infrastructure have posi-
tioned ML/MM calculations as a cost-effective yet accurate alternative to the well-established
QM/MM methods. 14,15
   The idea behind QM/MM calculations is to model a small region of the system (typically
O ∼ 101 −102 atoms) using highly accurate but computationally expensive QM techniques,

                                                2
 while the remainder of the system is described using less accurate but computationally
inexpensive MM FFs. Current QM/MM studies mostly employ electrostatic embedding (EE)
strategies to describe the interactions between the QM and MM regions. In these approaches,
the MM point charge environment is explicitly included in the QM calculations, leading to
polarized wavefunctions or electronic density. Additionally, the van der Waals (vdW) and
short-range exchange-repulsion interactions between the QM and MM regions are described
utilizing MM-based functional forms. These methods have proved their success at various
applications, 16–19 being generally superior to mechanical embedding (ME) strategies, where
QM-MM intermolecular interactions remain fully represented at the MM level. 20,21
   In the context of ML/MM simulations, interactions between the ML and MM regions
have predominantly been treated using ME schemes. 1,22–25 These schemes typically rely on
Lennard-Jones (LJ) and Coulomb terms to model vdW and electrostatic interactions between
the ML and MM regions. A recent absolute hydration free energy (AHFE) benchmark 26 on
the FreeSolv database, 27 comparing the performance of ME ML/MM (ANI-2x/OpenFF-
2.0.0 28 ) with fully MM (OpenFF-2.0.0 and CHARMM 29 ) predictions, generally found no
improvement in predictive performance when using hybrid ML methods, except for highly
flexible molecules.
   Furthermore, the literature presents mixed conclusions regarding the performance of these
simulations in modeling protein-ligand binding affinities. For example, while some studies
report improved accuracy compared to OpenFF-1.0.0 30,31 and GAFF2, 32 a recent report 33
failed to identify statistically significant differences in accuracy between ME ML/MM and
MM (OpenFF-2.2.0) relative binding free energy (RBFE) calculations. Since all these studies
report similar levels of accuracy for common protein benchmarks while using the same MLP
(ANI-2x 2 ), this suggests that the improvements reported earlier were likely due to deficiencies
in the reference FFs, which have been addressed with the update of the LJ parameters in
OpenFF-2.0.0 and later versions. Likewise, a separate RBFE benchmark 5 using the AceFF
1.0 MLP demonstrated improved accuracy compared to GAFF2, but correlation metrics


                                               3
 comparable to OPLS4. 34
   In a similar vein, other studies show that well-parameterized MM FFs perform compara-
bly to ME ML/MM methods. For example, optimal bespoke parameters for the intramolec-
ular terms of a GAFF-like FF produced conformational ensembles of fluorohydrins similar to
those obtained using ME ML/MM with ANI-2x. 25 Furthermore, refitting the torsional pa-
rameters of ligands yield consistent predictions compared to ME ML/MM with ANI-2x when
applying end-state corrections to calculate protein-ligand RBFEs. 33 Therefore, the overall
consensus seems to be that, for scenarios where MM FFs predict satisfactory intramolecu-
lar energies for the ligands and can generate relevant conformational ensembles, the use of
ME ML/MM offers little advantage, as protein-ligand (or solvent-ligand) interactions remain
represented at the MM level.
   In light of this, EE schemes, in which the MLP region can be polarized by the MM
environment, emerge as a promising approach to enhance this simplified ME representa-
tion. This is particularly relevant because, while full MLP simulations inherently account
for polarization and other many-body effects, their high computational cost still makes them
impractical for regular use and validation. Despite this, they have shown promise for model-
ing condensed-phase systems, with recent reports on AHFE calculations demonstrating their
ability to achieve highly accurate results for small organic molecules. 35,36
   Two main routes have been explored to incorporate the effect of the surrounding MM
environment on the MLP region. The first approach involves including (part of) the MM
environment as an additional input to the underlying ML model. This research avenue
is exemplified by methods such as FieldSchNet, 37 DPRc, 38 BuRNN, 39 and NepoIP. 40 The
main disadvantage of these models is their requirement to use environmental information
during training, which limits their transferability to other media and is associated with the
potentially higher computational costs of larger ML architectures and input data.
   Another line of research has focused on modeling how an MLP responds to its environ-
ment using physics-based methods. This has been approached by adapting the toolbox of


                                               4
 polarization methodologies developed over past decades, such as fluctuating charges, 41–43
Drude oscillators, 44,45 or Thole models, 46,47 and applying them atop MLPs. The various
transferable MLPs developed for organic molecules (e.g., ANI-2x, MACE-OFF, etc.) have
been the main target of these schemes. This is because deep neural network architectures
like ANI are short-ranged, considering only local chemical environments within ca. 3-6 Å
of a given atomic site, and are therefore unable to capture long-range interactions and en-
vironmental effects such as polarization. Furthermore, while graph-based, message-passing
architectures like MACE 48 and NequIP 49 have a longer receptive field, they still lack an
explicit treatment of electrostatics and dispersion.
   Efforts in this direction include the integration of MLPs into the AMOEBA polarizable
FF, 50,51 and direct-polarization approaches for EE ML/MM with ANI potentials. 52,53 Addi-
tionally, the electrostatic machine learning embedding (EMLE) model has recently emerged
as a promising and sophisticated approach. 54 Together with its associated emle-engine
package, 55 EMLE will be the focus of this study. By employing geometry-dependent charges
in conjunction with a Thole model, EMLE captures both the static and induced electro-
static responses of an MLP system to external MM fields. When combined with MLPs,
EMLE holds significant potential for improving accuracy in applications where current non-
polarizable, fixed-charge FFs fall short, such as simulations involving highly polar, charged,
or heterogeneous environments. 56–58 Importantly, EMLE is ML-region agnostic and can be
applied atop of any ML potential.
   In this study, we demonstrate robust training methodologies that achieve chemical ac-
curacy in ML/MM AHFEs calculations of small organic molecules using EMLE. This is
accomplished by combining MACE-OFF23(S) (and ANI-2x for the test dataset) and EMLE
for modeling the solute, TIP3P as the water model, and the LJ parameters from OpenFF-
2.0.0 where required. We show that training a bespoke EMLE model on Minimal Basis
Iterative Stockholder (MBIS) 59 decomposition of DFT densities and DFT dipolar polariz-
abilities enhances accuracy with respect to QM/MM. Additionally, we validate that refining


                                              5
 the EMLE parameters by fitting to the static and induced components derived from the
decomposition of QM/MM electrostatic interactions further improves accuracy, achieving
excellent agreement with QM/MM results.
   We also find that even EMLE models that perfectly reproduce QM/MM electrostatics
tend to overestimate AHFE predictions, making molecules overly hydrophilic. To correct
for this systematic error, which we primarily attribute to the double-counting of induction
interactions, we propose an empirical correction in the form of an effective dielectric constant.
This brings the AHFE predictions into closer agreement with experimental results. Finally,
we demonstrate that EMLE models are transferable between MLPs and to chemically related
molecules outside the training dataset.
   In association, we present two open-source software packages that are readily available to
the community: fes-ml, which enables hybrid ML/MM free energy calculations with support
for various alchemical modifications, and emle-bespoke, which streamlines the training of
EMLE models by automating conformer sampling, QM energy evaluations, and parameter
fitting, with modular components for flexible use. Altogether, the methods and software
presented in this study represent a significant step forward toward robust EE ML/MM
calculations.
   This paper is structured as follows. First, we present the free energy methods employed
to calculate the AHFEs for our 20-organic-molecule dataset and introduce the fes-ml pack-
age. Next, we describe the fundamental theory underlying the EMLE model and describe
strategies for improving the accuracy and precision of this embedding model, along with
the tools developed for this purpose. We then finely tune EMLE models, and apply them
in AHFE calculations, demonstrating systematic improvements in accuracy, with additional
enhancement observed upon introducing an effective dielectric constant in the final stage.
Finally, we demonstrate that our models are transferable to molecules outside the training
dataset, addressing cases where current nonpolarizable, fixed-charge FFs fall short in pre-
dicting AHFEs. The paper concludes with a discussion of our general findings and outlines


                                               6
 future research avenues for improving and applying EMLE as an EE model for ML/MM
simulations.

Training of EMLE Models

Training of bespoke EMLE models is a highly useful strategy for improving accuracy. It can
now be routinely performed by the user thanks to the recent overhaul of the emle-engine
package, which, among other features, introduced PyTorch-based routines that allow for the
efficient optimization of EMLE parameters. Here, we first review the main workflow that
underpins the training of EMLE models from QM data, and then present a “patching” proto-
col that can be used to further refine the EMLE predictions by fitting to the terms resulting
from the decomposition of the QM/MM electrostatic interaction. A diagram summarizing


                                               14
 these workflows is shown in Figure 2.
    The learnable parameters in the EMLE model are summarized in Table 1. Given a train-
ing dataset with arbitrary chemical structures, the local atomic environments are first featur-
ized using atomic environment vectors (AEVs), 76,77 which serve as the underlying chemical
descriptors. From these, a representative set of “basis vectors” is selected using the Infor-
mative Vector Machine. 78 These basis vectors are then used to construct Gaussian Process
Regression (GPR) models, which are employed on-the-fly during simulations to predict va-
lence widths and electronegativities, from which the remaining properties can be derived.

   In terms of computational cost, training and patching EMLE models is a highly attractive
option for small to medium-sized molecules, up to around 100 atoms. The primary bottleneck
lies in generating reference data. However, an accurate bespoke EMLE model can typically be
trained using ca. 10-100 relevant conformations. Assuming only elements commonly found
in drug-like molecules are present, each of the required DFT calculations can be performed
in a matter of minutes when using multiple CPU cores. This enables model training on the

                                                 17

been generated, the training and patching stages themselves take only a few minutes. Given
the simulation performance currently achieved when pairing EMLE with standard MLPs
(e.g., 1-5 ns/day with MACE-OFF23(S) on a modern GPU), the cost of training is, in most
cases, significantly lower than the cost of running production simulations. As such, training
a bespoke model is strongly recommended if preliminary results using the general EMLE
model are suboptimal.

   We used the emle-bespoke package to train all EMLE models in this study. emle-bespoke
is a Python software package we developed for training and patching EMLE models. The

 source code, examples, and documentation are available at https://github.com/michellab/
emle-bespoke. We trained models in two iterations. The first used only configurations
sampled at the ME ML/MM level, and the second added configurations sampled at the EE

the possibility that this may not hold for more complex chemical systems.



Results and Discussion

Bespoke and Patched EMLE Models Enhance QM/MM Agreement

To assess the accuracy of the bespoke and patched EMLE models in predicting QM/MM
electrostatic interaction energies for the 20-molecule dataset in Figure 1B, we evaluate their
performance on a dataset comprised of 6000 configurations unseen during training (Figure
3A). Furthermore, we compare EMLE predictions to MBIS-derived valence widths and total
charges, and assess how well EMLE reproduces molecular DFT polarizabilities (Figure 3B).
The reference DFT level of theory used throughout this study is B3LYP/cc-pVTZ, the same
used to generate the reference data of the QM7 dataset for training the general EMLE
model. 54
   Figure 3A compares the performance of the general, bespoke and patched models in
reproducing the total QM/MM electrostatic interaction energy. The distributions show that
the patched model matches or improves upon all error and correlation metrics compared to
the bespoke model, which in turn outperforms the general model. Importantly, the bespoke
model corrects the underestimated energy predictions of the general model (outliers above the
x = y line), which correspond to water configurations (absent in the QM7 dataset). However,


                                             19
 while the overall model’s accuracy improves, the bespoke model still shows a tendency for
slightly overestimating the interaction energy. This can be visually seen for the strongest
interactions (more negative energies) and is also captured by the -0.49 kcal/mol mean signed
error (MSE). This systematic bias mostly comes from the static component, as can be seen
by inspecting the equivalent plots of Figure 3A for the static (Figure S5) and induced (Figure
S6) components of the electrostatic interaction.
    This overestimation of the electrostatic interaction energy seen for the bespoke model
is mitigated when the model is patched. This is because fitting aQEq and χ to match
  QM/M M
Estatic    results in effective charges that more accurately capture higher-order moments
in the ESP multipole expansion, likely correcting for the know overestimation of molecu-
lar dipoles and quadrupole moments by MBIS-derived atomic charges. 79 As shown in the
molecule-by-molecule results (Figures S9 and S10), this fine-tuning primarily improves accu-
racy for polar molecules with significant dipole moments, such as water, alcohols, aldehydes,
ketones, esters, ethers, carboxylic acids, and amides, while being less significant for apolar or
purely aromatic compounds, such as n-pentane, n-octane, benzene, or naphthalene. These
observations support the importance of refining charges to better reproduce the molecular
                            QM/M M
ESP, either by fitting to Estatic    (this study) or directly to the vacuum QM ESP. Note that
the patched model was trained with regularization (η = 1.0 in eq 17), so we hypothesize that
its accuracy could be further improved by reducing the regularization strength. However, too
weak a regularization may lead to typical RESP-related issues, where the charges become
overly sensitive to molecular geometry. This risk can be mitigated by training on multiple
configurations simultaneously, as is done here.
    In agreement with the conclusions of previous reports, 54 the error in the interaction
energy is dominated by the static component (Figure S5) rather than by the induced com-
ponent (Figure S6), with root mean square errors (RMSEs) being 3 to 4 times larger for
the static component (for the general model, up to 2.44 kcal/mol). This issue is particularly
significant for molecules with large partial charges (typical in polar functional groups), as the


                                               20
 lowest possible scaling for interactions involving charges is r−1 (charge-charge), whereas for
interactions involving induced dipoles, it is r−4 (charge-induced dipole). Consequently, inac-
curacies in charge predictions (particularly valence charges, as core charges remain relatively
constant) propagate over larger distances, thus affecting a greater number of interactions.
   Since the polarization response errors are in general quite small, fitting aT hole and kZ
            QM/M M
to match Eind        (patched models) or α (bespoke models) only marginally improved the
accuracy of the induction predictions relative to the general model (ca. 0.1–0.2 kcal/mol).
This reinforces the importance of accurately describing the static electrostatic interactions,
motivating for a careful treatment of that component in future training of general EMLE
models through inclusion of information about in vacuo molecular ESPs. Alternatively,
explicit static atomic dipoles could be incorporated into EMLE to avoid the need for charge
refitting via the static ESP workaround. Moreover, this result suggests that patching the
induced component of the models using eq 9 can be avoided altogether, especially considering
the potential charge spill-out issues that this step may introduce (not present here, as can
be seen by the similarity of the molecular polarizability distributions for the bespoke and
patched models in Figure 3B).
   Although the general model was trained on a more chemically diverse dataset (QM7) than
the one used in this study, it exhibits poorer performance across all statistical metrics when
compared to the bespoke and patched models. This can be attributed to sparse coverage of
configurational space, as the QM7 dataset provides only a single minimized conformation per
molecule, 81,82 lacking thermalized structures (e.g., those sampled along normal modes). Since
EMLE predicts geometry-dependent charges, this highlights the importance of including
diverse conformer geometries in the training of future general EMLE models. This diversity
is essential for accurately capturing charge nonlocality, particularly the influence of highly
electronegative groups located multiple bonds away. Additionally, we cannot rule out the
possibility that the underlying GPR model is unable to generalize effectively for large and
diverse training datasets.


                                              21
    In terms of the agreement between EMLE predictions and MBIS valence widths and total
charges (Figure 3B), the bespoke models perform best, as expected, since these properties
are used as target values in this training step. The error in the general EMLE model is
particularly significant for sulfur, as its total charges are severely overestimated and valence
widths underestimated (these are coupled parameters in EMLE). Although the charges in
the patched model tend to deviate slightly more from the MBIS values than in the bespoke
model, the adjustments needed to improve the static interactions are generally small. Hence,
MBIS charges serve as excellent initial guesses for further optimization and can also act as
regularization references. Preliminary tests indicate that optimizing s can further enhance
the accuracy of electrostatic interactions. However, in this study, we aimed to minimize the
coupling between the optimization of static and induced components in EMLE, as these are
inherently coupled due to the need to use s and qval to compute atomic volumes. Further
                                                      QM/M M
analysis of optimizing both s and qcore to improve Estatic     is left for future studies. Lastly,
molecular polarizabilities are reproduced with similar levels of accuracy across all models.
   Overall, these results support the idea that, for fragments commonly found in drug-
like molecules, (1) EMLE’s embedding model captures sufficient physics to reproduce the
QM-polarized electrostatic response, and (2) given relevant conformational ensembles, the
underlying ML model is flexible enough to accurately learn the required parameters to handle
the chemical diversity present in our training dataset.

EMLE Enables HFE Predictions with Chemical Accuracy

To assess the accuracy of EMLE in predicting AHFEs, we compare its predictions to exper-
imental data. The accuracy of these calculations is influenced by three main factors: (1) the
accuracy of the molecular model, (2) the completeness of the configurational sampling, and
(3) the reliability of the underlying perturbation protocol. The flexible molecules in Figure
1B only possess low-energy torsional barriers, and thus no enhanced sampling techniques
are required for a comprehensive exploration of their configurational space. Furthermore, we


                                                                                                                    23
 have verified that our chosen perturbation protocol provides sufficient phase space overlap
between λ-windows, mitigating concerns about the robustness of our free energy estimations
(Figure S11). Given these conditions, we attribute the accuracy of the AHFE calculations
presented next primarily to the performance of the underlying model. This allows us to
directly evaluate the accuracy limits of EMLE in AHFE calculations and compare its per-
formance to that of other state-of-the-art methods.
   The AHFE results for various models considered in this study are shown in Figure 4. The
values given in square brackets indicate the 95% confidence interval obtained via bootstrap-
ping. OpenFF/TIP3P is the model that performs best overall (RMSE = 0.80 [0.62, 0.96]
kcal/mol; mean signed error, MSE = 0.23 [-0.12, 0.56] kcal/mol; mean unsigned error, MUE
= 0.68 [0.50, 0.86]; coefficient of determination, R2 = 0.95 [0.86,0.98], Pearson’s ρ = 0.97
[0.92, 0.99], and Kendall’s τ = 0.86 [0.79, 0.98]). The ME model (Figure S12) closely follows
the OpenFF/TIP3P performance, not exhibiting a statistically significant improvement at
95% confidence level (see one-sided Wilcoxon p-values in Figure S14). This agrees with a
recent report, 26 which indicates that ME in the context of ML/MM provides significant im-
provements only for flexible solutes where intramolecular energetics are poorly described by
MM FFs.
   The predictions of the general EMLE model are in poor agreement with experiment
(RMSE = 3.20 [2.08, 4.27] kcal/mol, MUE = 2.46 [1.64, 3.43] kcal/mol, MSE = -2.00 [-
3.14, -0.94] kcal/mol), with unsigned errors as large as 8.29 kcal/mol for acetic acid. We
anticipate that this limitation is not restricted to AHFE calculations and therefore do not
recommend the out-of-the-box application of EE methods for protein-ligand binding free
energy simulations, as similar performance issues are expected. However, this significantly
changes for both the bespoke and patched models. Despite performing worse on error metrics
compared to OpenFF/TIP3P, these models exhibit similar correlations across R2 , ρ, and τ .
Importantly, both the bespoke (RMSE = 2.40 [1.84, 2.89] kcal/mol, MUE = 2.01 [1.43, 2.59]
kcal/mol, MSE = -1.93 [-2.55, -1.29] kcal/mol) and patched models (RMSE = 1.63 [1.30,


                                             24
 1.93] kcal/mol, MUE = 1.41 [1.06, 1.77] kcal/mol, MSE = -1.39 [-1.76, -1.02] kcal/mol) show
significant improvements in error metrics compared to the general model, with the patched
model performing statistically significantly better than both the bespoke and general models
at the 95% confidence level. This supports the improved QM/MM agreement observed
in the previous subsection and suggests that better alignment with QM/MM electrostatic
interaction energies enhances the performance of EMLE models relative to experimental
values at the DFT level considered in this study.
   Nevertheless, despite the excellent agreement of the patched EMLE model with reference
QM/MM calculations, this does not directly translate to equally good agreement with exper-
imental HFE data. A systematic negative bias is observed, indicating that the molecules are
predicted to be too hydrophilic. However, the high correlations found in these models imply
that this systematic error could, in principle, be corrected by tuning the effective dielectric
constant proposed in eq 13. This is feasible since the MM→ML/MM corrections are mostly
negative (Figure S13) and can therefore be attenuated.

                                                                                                                28
    Using an effective dielectric constant (ϵ > 1) in eq (13) can be interpreted interchangeably
as either damping the external MM field or scaling the induction interactions (i.e., the
polarization response). Damping the MM field can help mitigate overly strong electric fields
that arise due to: (1) overestimated partial charges for the solvent, (2) artificially high
charge densities resulting from the point-charge representation, and (3) the inability of fixed-
charge models to properly respond to changes in the polarity of their microenvironment. 83–85
These issues are particularly significant at the solute-solvent interface, forming the primary
motivation for buffered ML/MM approaches, 39 which shift the interface away from the solute
region.
   On the other hand, interpreting the use of an effective dielectric constant as scaling the
induction interactions is especially relevant because it is well-known that the C6 dispersion
coefficients of nonpolarizable MM FFs tend to be spuriously large. 70,86 This has been mainly
attributed to (1) the neglect of higher-order dispersion terms (C8 , C10 , etc.), (2) the lack
of explicit polarization, or (3) other missing intermolecular interactions captured by the LJ
potential, which is typically the last component to be fitted. Since Debye interactions (and
possibly other higher-order induction effects) scale roughly as r−6 , they may be partially
represented by the long-range LJ potential. Therefore, LJ parameters derived from nonpo-
larizable FFs are inherently incompatible with polarizable schemes such as EMLE, since they
are fitted to reproduce empirical liquid properties, 28 implicitly incorporating some induction
effects 71–73 not included in the effective charges.
   Here, we primarily attribute the overestimation of AHFEs by EMLE to the spurious
double-counting of induction interactions. We hypothesize that this arises because the LJ pa-
rameters in OpenFF were fitted to experimental condensed-phase properties, which may have
caused them to implicitly capture some polarization effects. Furthermore, it remains an open
question which combinations of DFT functionals and basis sets provide sufficiently accurate
HFE calculations without a scaling constant, as most were not developed for condensed-phase
dynamics, and recent reports indicate that the accuracy of relative solvation free energies


                                                29
 depends significantly on their choice. 87 Incidentally, a similar systematic overestimation of
AHFEs to the one we observe has been reported in a previous QM/MM study using CGenFF
with TIP3P LJ parameters, where the HFE bias became progressively more negative with
increasing ratios of Hartree-Fock exact exchange. 88 Overall, these observations motivate the
development of LJ parameter sets explicitly designed for compatibility with EMLE.


EMLE Models Are Transferable and Accurate

Using the patched EMLE model with ϵ−1 = 0.6 from the previous sections, we evaluate
its performance, without further refinement, on a set of small, drug-like fragments that are
known to challenge MM and ME ML/MM approaches. These molecules, extracted from the
FreeSolv database, 27 exhibit chemistry similar to that of the training set shown in Figure 1B.
To ensure consistency, all simulation settings were retained from the previous calculations. In
addition to employing the MACE-OFF23(S) MLP, for which the effective dielectric constant
was tuned, we also tested the EMLE patched model in combination with MACE-OFF24(M)
and ANI-2x. The signed errors relative to experiment are presented in Figure 6.

2x models arise for polyhydroxy alkanes, where a critical interplay exists between intra-
and intermolecular hydrogen bonding. This stresses the importance of the underlying MLP
in determining simulation accuracy, particularly in capturing conformational preferences
such as hydroxyl group orientation, which directly affect HFE values. 26 For rigid molecules
(mobley_242480 and mobley_7378987), however, all EE models performs essentially equiv-
alently. Overall, the improvement achieved by the EE models over both OpenFF/TIP3P
(RMSE = 3.87 kcal/mol) and the ME ML/MM models (MACE-OFF23(S) RMSE = 3.91
kcal/mol, MACE-OFF24(M) RMSE = 3.77 kcal/mol, ANI-2x RMSE = 3.33 kcal/mol) is


                                            31
 substantial, underlining the importance of explicitly accounting for polarization.
   The MLP-agnostic nature of the EMLE models is expected, as no MLP-specific infor-
mation is used during training, i.e., only QM/MBIS and conformational data are provided.
This property supports transferability not only to chemically related molecules outside the
training set but also across different MLPs. Furthermore, the strong agreement with exper-
iment observed for both EE ANI-2x and EE MACE-OFF24(M) without reoptimizing the
dielectric constant suggests that the empirical scaling primarily compensates for deficiencies
in the MM/ML interactions (e.g., LJ terms) rather than errors in the MLP itself. Finally, we
note that the EMLE models developed here are unlikely to generalize to molecules that are
chemically very different from those in the training set. Developing a general EMLE model
trained on a larger, chemically diverse dataset, while incorporating the ideas presented in
this work, would therefore be a welcome next step.



Conclusion

This study has presented methodologies for training EMLE models, demonstrating that the
inclusion of polarization in ML/MM simulations is important for accurately predicting HFEs.
Incorporating polarization enables EMLE models to be competitive with, and in some cases
outperform, state-of-the-art methods, particularly in systems where those methods fall short.
   We trained our models on a dataset of 20 small organic molecules and showed that
EMLE models can achieve chemical accuracy with minimal empirical fitting, using only a
single scaling parameter. Additionally, we evaluated the models on unseen molecules, where
they demonstrated strong transferability and maintained high accuracy.
   Overall, this study provides key insights into the fundamental considerations that should
be taken into account when developing EE schemes for ML/MM simulations, and offers
strategies for achieving robust modeling of drug-like molecules. The main conclusions of this
work are as follows:



                                             32
    • Bespoke and patched EMLE training protocols generate models that accurately repro-
     duce DFT QM/MM interaction energies. These models show excellent agreement with
     reference QM/MM calculations.

   • EMLE models that accurately reproduce intermolecular QM/MM electrostatic inter-
     actions exhibit improved accuracy and correlation with experimental HFE data, but
     still show systematic errors towards overly negative HFE predictions.

   • This systematic negative bias, primarily attributed to the double-counting of induction
     interactions, can be corrected by damping the polarization response using an effective
     dielectric constant. A value of ϵ−1 = 0.6 yields AHFE predictions within chemical
     accuracy.

   • Well-calibrated EMLE models are transferable across chemically related molecules and
     between different MLPs. They outperform MM FFs and ME ML/MM approaches in
     challenging systems, although final simulation accuracy may still depend on the quality
     of the underlying MLP.


   Alongside the presented protocols and results, we have introduced two software pack-
ages: fes-ml (https://github.com/michellab/fes-ml), a toolkit for running ML/MM
HFE calculations, and emle-bespoke (https://github.com/michellab/emle-bespoke), a
package for training and patching bespoke EMLE models.
   Future work will focus on developing EMLE-compatible LJ parameters to achieve a more
physically grounded improvement of ML-MM interactions without relying on empirical ad-
justments. We will also assess the transferability of the training protocols to diverse solvent
and protein environments, noting that the applicability of the patched EMLE models beyond
aqueous systems remains to be explicitly tested.

This working note records an executed classical calculation, not a quantum run.

Question changed
The initial scan asked whether more accurate ADAPT-QSCI energies might improve
EMLE induction labels and hydration. Inherited branch evidence shows that this
requires separate physical-reference and static/induced convergence tests.
The new bounded test asks whether energy and induction convergence can conceal
static error on an actual embedded molecular Hamiltonian, even under ideal
deterministic selection of the exact input-state probabilities.

Input and model
Inherited water record 1926 is read from
branches/branch-3/ada/review2/selected-records.json, corresponding to branch-3
ledger 79. The raw published dataset provenance and units are described in
branches/branch-3/ada/review2/V7-reference-audit.txt:4-9,18-42.
No geometry, charge, cutoff, periodic convention or empirical dielectric is changed.
New input copy: water-1926-input.json. Input/source/script hashes, package versions,
convergence, fixed orbitals and energy constants are in water_selector_result.json.
The input is neutral singlet water with fixed vacuum canonical RHF/cc-pVTZ orbitals.
O 1s (orbital 0) is inactive. Orbitals 1-6 define CAS(8e,6o), with four alpha and
four beta electrons and 225 determinants. No orbital optimisation or external
response correction is applied after vacuum RHF. This is a deliberately limited
physical Hamiltonian, consistent with the inherited reference-adequacy negatives.

Implementation and verification
water_selector.py:23-55 constructs vacuum, half-field and full-field matrices.
Inactive-electron and nuclear/MM terms enter the scalar core energy and projected
one-electron Hamiltonian. Full two-electron terms use the same orbitals throughout.
Matrices are symmetric within 1e-11 Hartree; half-field affine agreement is
1.99e-13 Hartree. Dense ground energies at vacuum and full field agree with the
PySCF CASCI iterative solver to about 3e-14 Hartree. This is a different solver
path through the same integrals, not independent integral generation.
The parent gaps are 0.29720, 0.33037 and 0.36461 Hartree at the three fields;
the lowest state is therefore separated within the computed sector.
Wall time was 0.55 seconds in the existing isolated environment, including
reference diagonalisation and all selector cases. It is an indication, not
a realistic resource estimate or quantum/comparator performance ratio.

Define \(V=H(1)-H(0)\). The direct vacuum expectation and induction are
\[D=\langle u_0|V|u_0\rangle=-35.353024\ \mathrm{kcal/mol},\]
\[I=E(1)-E(0)-D=-3.004491\ \mathrm{kcal/mol}.\]

branches/branch-3/ada/review2/reproduction.csv:3 are \(-34.101718\) static and
\(-7.519022\) induced kcal/mol. Compact CAS differs by \(-1.251306\) and
\(+4.514532\), respectively, and has about 40 percent of the magnitude of
that induction. This is a discrepancy between specified references, not an
error bound to exact chemistry or a claim that B3LYP5 is more accurate.
It supports withholding physical-target replacement status from this space.

Exact parent ground probabilities at each field are the ideal test oracle.
Vacuum-only and field-only spaces take the largest \(R\) probabilities.
Pool candidates are the union of the three top-\(R\) lists, truncated back
to \(R\) by equal-weight summed probabilities; ties use determinant index.
This is not a finite-shot sample, an ADAPT-QSCI state or response-aware SCI.
The raw pool dimensions at \(R=8,16,32\) are 12,19,36, respectively.
All endpoint diagonalisation and the static expectation use each selected

  "branches/branch-3/ada/review2/V7-reference-audit.txt": "V7: six-snapshot reference reproduction and correlated comparison

Sources and execution
Source data: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/michellab/EMLE_HFE_SI/0279424ec1770e155533af6247f28ebca98b72b5/data/testing_datasets/testing_data_iter1.pkl
SHA256: 4328e00ac747df3609ec72dedf5a82c5acba539ebbec5fe5f97aee9a00956235
Existing evidence is reused read-only from emmy/review1. The source hash is asserted before restricted reading.
Only the four NumPy globals previously opcode-audited in entry 42 are permitted.
Scripts are outside the data directory, in ada/review2, and run with Python -I.
Isolated uv environment: Python 3.12.13, PySCF 2.14.0, NumPy 2.5.3, SciPy 1.18.1, h5py 3.16.0, LibXC 7.0.0.
The macOS PySCF wheel reports no OpenMP; effective PySCF thread count is 1 despite requesting 2.
Commands: venv/bin/python -I reference_audit.py --method b3lyp5
          venv/bin/python -I reference_audit.py --method b3lyp5 --level 5 --record 4
          venv/bin/python -I reference_audit.py --method mp2 --tight
          venv/bin/python -I tabulate_audit.py
Paths in these commands are relative to ada/review2. Exact executable source is reference_audit.py.
Outputs include each run's energies, timings, convergence choice and decomposition; provenance.json hashes scripts/results.

Selection and units
Each molecular composition has 100 records. Indices are zero-based global pickle indices.
Within each formula group choose the observed induction nearest its median, 1st percentile and 75th percentile.
Water: 1912, 1926, 1951. Methanol: 935, 909, 992, respectively.
These are deliberately selected records, not random draws or an unbiased ensemble.
Coordinate distances support Angstrom units: nearest H-O distances 0.9452 to 1.0056.
Every retained MM atom has a nearest-solute distance below 12 Angstrom, matching Q's atomwise cutoff.
The truncated MM charge sets have nonzero net charges; no neutralisation, recentering or new cutoff is applied.
Record geometries and charges are saved in selected-records.json; geometrical checks are in input-geometry-checks.json.
Labels are kJ/mol, as established by the author notebook conversion in entry 42; report tables use kcal/mol.
Hartree conversion used: 2625.4996394799 kJ/mol. No MM self-energy or LJ energy is included.

Decomposition and nuclear conventions
At fixed geometry define \(H(s)=H_0+sV\), where the MM charges multiply by physical perturbation strength \(s\).
PySCF qmmm includes both electronic attraction and the solute-nuclear/MM scalar in total energy.
Official implementation description: https://pyscf.org/pyscf_api_docs/pyscf.qmmm.html
The static term is \(D=\operatorname{Tr}(\gamma_0 v_{\rm MM})+N_{\rm MM}\).
The induced term is \(I=E(1)-E(0)-D\), following Q eq16, primary ada/Q-accepted-layout.txt:615-637.
Electronic-only convention uses \(D_e=D-N_{\rm MM}\) and \(\Delta E_e=E(1)-E(0)-N_{\rm MM}\).
Thus \(\Delta E_e-D_e=I\): consistent removal cancels from induction.
Removing nuclear electrostatics only from static while retaining total embedded energy is inconsistent and fails badly.
reproduction.csv:2-7 contains labels, both static conventions, both consistent induction conventions and residuals.
The static labels clearly include nuclear electrostatics: electronic-only values range -1644.64 to +482.02 kcal/mol,
whereas matching total static values range -34.10 to -9.96 kcal/mol.
This pins down these records' decomposition convention, not all production simulation conventions.

DFT reproduction
Basis: spherical cc-pVTZ, all atoms and retained point charges, neutral singlets, no density fitting, no frozen orbitals.
Predeclared reproduction tolerance was 0.02 kcal/mol per component (entry 70); all six pass.
Default PySCF b3lyp also passes but is the VWN-RPA/Gaussian variant, not ORCA's default VWN5.
ORCA manual: https://www.faccts.de/docs/orca/6.1/manual/contents/modelchemistries/DensityFunctionalTheory.html
PySCF explicit b3lyp5 definition: https://pyscf.org/_modules/pyscf/dft/libxc.html
Use b3lyp5 for the component comparison. Static residual range -0.004936 to -0.000230 kcal/mol;
induction residual range +0.000966 to +0.004493 kcal/mol. Maximum residual is below 0.005.
PySCF grid level 4; SCF energy tolerance 1e-11 Hartree. Strong methanol grid level 5 check changes
static by -0.000001821 and induction by -0.000000188 kcal/mol, much smaller than label residuals.
Original ORCA grid, exact version, possible integral approximations and generating scripts remain unavailable.
Residuals are therefore not attributed solely to grid or functional differences; this is tolerance reproduction.

Correlated follow-up
MP2 with RHF orbitals uses full cc-pVTZ and all electrons, at unchanged geometry and point-charge field.
Official method documentation: https://pyscf.org/user/mp.html
Static term comes from relaxed total-energy response: \(D_h=[E(h)-E(-h)]/(2h)\).
No unrelaxed MP2 density is substituted for the derivative. Induction is again \(E(1)-E(0)-D_h\).
Use \(h=0.0005\), checked against \(h=0.001\); tightened SCF energy tolerance 1e-13 Hartree and gradient 1e-9.
Step-size discrepancy is below 0.00000081 kcal/mol for every record.
An initial less-tight run for water 1951 differed by about 0.00146 kcal/mol in the derivative;
the tightened rerun resolves this and its raw initial output is preserved.
correlated-differences.csv:2-7 gives MP2 values, MP2-minus-B3LYP5 static/induced/total changes and step-size checks.
Water static shifts: -0.3263, -0.6206, -0.3842; induced shifts: +0.0960, +0.1835, +0.0728 kcal/mol.
Methanol static shifts: -0.4573, -0.4821, -0.1121; induced shifts: +0.0745, +0.1112, +0.0302 kcal/mol.
All selected total electrostatic shifts are negative, ranging -0.4371 to -0.0820 kcal/mol.
Static and induction shifts oppose each other; a response-only reference replacement misses this feature.

Scope
MP2 establishes a nonzero correlated-versus-DFT reference change for these records, not improved physical accuracy.
No higher-order correlated-method convergence, complete-basis convergence, solvent back-polarisation or spill-out audit is claimed.
A handful of selected snapshots is not an ensemble result, hydration prediction, quantum calculation or quantum-cost result.
Do not extrapolate these changes to Q's 0.6 empirical scaling or the hydration bias.
Compare with EMLE fit residuals only descriptively, and retain static-density/LJ alternatives and ensemble requirements.
The narrow next question is response-certified selection at identical physical Hamiltonians and fair total cost.
No scientific verdict on double counting, publication novelty or quantum advantage is assigned.

  "branches/branch-3/ada/review2/reference_audit.py": "import argparse, hashlib, io, json, pickle, platform, time
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pyscf
from pyscf import gto, dft, scf, qmmm, mp, lib

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SOURCE = ROOT.parent.parent / 'emmy/review1/testing_data_iter1.pkl'
ALLOWED = {('numpy.core.multiarray', '_reconstruct'): np._core.multiarray._reconstruct,
           ('numpy.core.multiarray', 'scalar'): np._core.multiarray.scalar,
           ('numpy', 'ndarray'): np.ndarray, ('numpy', 'dtype'): np.dtype}
class Restricted(pickle.Unpickler):
    def find_class(self, module, name):
        if (module, name) not in ALLOWED:
            raise pickle.UnpicklingError(f'Forbidden global {module}.{name}')
        return ALLOWED[module, name]

def select():
    raw = SOURCE.read_bytes()
    assert hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest() == '4328e00ac747df3609ec72dedf5a82c5acba539ebbec5fe5f97aee9a00956235'
    data = Restricted(io.BytesIO(raw)).load()
    records = []
    for name, composition in [('water', [1,1,8]), ('methanol', [1,1,1,1,6,8])]:
        indices = [i for i,z in enumerate(data['z']) if sorted(map(int,z)) == composition]
        labels = np.array([data['e_ind'][i] for i in indices])
        for role, quantile in [('median',.5), ('p01',.01), ('p75',.75)]:
            target = np.quantile(labels,quantile)
            i = indices[int(np.argmin(abs(labels-target)))]
            records.append(dict(name=name, role=role, index=i, z=np.asarray(data['z'][i]).tolist(),
                xyz_qm=np.asarray(data['xyz_qm'][i]).tolist(), xyz_mm=np.asarray(data['xyz_mm'][i]).tolist(),
                charges_mm=np.asarray(data['charges_mm'][i]).tolist(),
                label_static_kj=float(data['e_static'][i]),label_ind_kj=float(data['e_ind'][i])))
    return records

def run(record, method='b3lyp', level=4, tight=False):
    start=time.time()
    mol=gto.M(atom=list(zip(record['z'],record['xyz_qm'])), basis='cc-pvtz',unit='Angstrom',
              charge=0,spin=0,verbose=0,max_memory=2000)
    coords=np.asarray(record['xyz_mm']);charges=np.asarray(record['charges_mm'])
    def solve(s):
        mf = dft.RKS(mol) if method.startswith('b3') else scf.RHF(mol)
        if method.startswith('b3'):
            mf.xc=method; mf.grids.level=level
        mf.conv_tol=1e-13 if tight else 1e-11
        if tight: mf.conv_tol_grad=1e-9
        mf.max_cycle=150
        if s: mf=qmmm.mm_charge(mf, coords, charges*s, unit='Angstrom')
        mf.kernel()
        if not mf.converged: raise RuntimeError('SCF not converged')
        if method=='mp2':
            pt=mp.MP2(mf);pt.kernel();return mf, float(pt.e_tot)
        return mf,float(mf.e_tot)
    vacuum,e0=solve(0)
    embedded,e1=solve(1)
    hpert=embedded.get_hcore()-vacuum.get_hcore()
    nuclear=float(embedded.energy_nuc()-mol.energy_nuc())
    electronic=float(np.einsum('ij,ji',hpert,vacuum.make_rdm1()))
    if method=='mp2':
        # Central derivative of total MP2 energy supplies relaxed static response.
        derivatives={}
        for h in (.001,.0005):
            _,ep=solve(h);_,em=solve(-h);derivatives[str(h)]=(ep-em)/(2*h)
        static=derivatives['0.0005']; electronic=static-nuclear
    else: static=electronic+nuclear; derivatives={}
    factor=2625.4996394799
    result=dict(name=record['name'],role=record['role'],index=record['index'],method=method,
        grid_level=level if method.startswith('b3') else None,nao=mol.nao_nr(),mm_count=len(charges),
        vacuum_hartree=e0,embedded_hartree=e1,nuclear_mm_hartree=nuclear,
        static_with_nuclear_kj=static*factor,static_without_nuclear_kj=electronic*factor,
        induced_consistent_kj=(e1-e0-static)*factor,
        induced_without_nuclear_consistent_kj=(e1-e0-nuclear-electronic)*factor,
        induced_omit_static_nuclear_only_kj=(e1-e0-electronic)*factor,
        derivatives_hartree=derivatives,seconds=time.time()-start,scf_tight=tight,
        label_static_kj=record['label_static_kj'],label_ind_kj=record['label_ind_kj'])
    result['static_error_kcal']=(result['static_with_nuclear_kj']-record['label_static_kj'])/4.184
    result['ind_error_kcal']=(result['induced_consistent_kj']-record['label_ind_kj'])/4.184
    return result

if __name__=='__main__':
    p=argparse.ArgumentParser();p.add_argument('--method',default='b3lyp');p.add_argument('--level',type=int,default=4)
    p.add_argument('--record',type=int);p.add_argument('--tight',action='store_true');args=p.parse_args();lib.num_threads(2)
    records=select()
    (ROOT/'selected-records.json').write_text(json.dumps(records,indent=2))
    (ROOT/'runtime.json').write_text(json.dumps(dict(python=platform.python_version(),pyscf=pyscf.__version__,numpy=np.__version__,libxc=dft.libxc.__version__,threads=lib.num_threads(),source_sha256=hashlib.sha256(SOURCE.read_bytes()).hexdigest()),indent=2))
    for j,record in enumerate(records):
        if args.record is not None and j!=args.record:continue
        result=run(record,args.method,args.level,args.tight)
        path=ROOT/f"result-{j}-{args.method}-grid{args.level}{'-tight' if args.tight else ''}.json"
        path.write_text(json.dumps(result,indent=2));print(json.dumps(result),flush=True)
